meta.query: Clinical nephrology — RCTs, systematic reviews & meta-analyses (humans, English)
meta.source: PubMed (NLM) abstracts; summaries and appraisals generated automatically from those abstracts. Each entry links to its PubMed record and DOI.
meta.note: Summaries and PICO are machine analyses of the source abstracts; criteria marked “not specified” were not stated. Read the source before acting clinically.

articles.authors: Cai W, Wang D, Zhu L, Liu X
articles.title: Risk factors for acute kidney injury after pediatric liver transplantation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 retrospective cohort studies involving 2,986 pediatric liver transplant recipients to evaluate the incidence and risk factors of acute kidney injury (AKI) following pediatric liver transplantation (PLT).

pico.intervention: Perioperative and patient-related risk factors (e.g., preoperative hepatic impairment, coagulation abnormalities, inadequate nutrition and oxygen delivery, intraoperative blood loss, transfusion burden, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and postoperative organ support)
pico.outcome: Incidence of postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI)

inclusion: Observational studies on risk factors for AKI following pediatric liver transplantation published from database inception to September 2025

appraisal.bottom_line: The pooled incidence rate of AKI following pediatric liver transplantation is high at 30.7% (95% CI: 25.0% to 36.3%). While multiple perioperative and patient-related factors are associated with postoperative AKI, many of these associations are based on a small number of studies and require cautious interpretation.
appraisal.relevance: Enables pediatric nephrologists and transplant surgeons to identify high-risk pediatric liver transplant recipients early and implement targeted perioperative management strategies to mitigate AKI risk.
appraisal.caveat: The analysis is entirely based on retrospective cohort studies, which limits the ability to establish causal relationships. Furthermore, many individual risk factors were evaluated in only a small number of studies, and the authors note a critical need for large-scale prospective validation.

articles.authors: Beresford L, Burgess LC, Dewhurst S, Hutchison A, Pandyan AD et al.
articles.title: Lower-limb neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) for adults with kidney failure undergoing dialysis.
articles.summary: A Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (348 eligible participants, 299 analyzed) evaluating the efficacy and safety of lower-limb neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) in adults with kidney failure undergoing dialysis.

pico.population: Adults (aged 18 years or older) with kidney failure receiving hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis
pico.intervention: Lower-limb neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) training programmes delivered via surface electrodes
pico.comparison: No NMES (usual care, sham NMES, or exercise with a usual care control)
pico.outcome: Critical outcomes (life participation, cardiovascular outcomes [blood pressure, resting heart rate], death, fatigue, pain, infection, vascular access problems) and important outcomes (muscle function, functional performance, muscle structure, quality of life, biochemical/hormonal markers, treatment experience)

inclusion: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster RCTs evaluating lower-limb NMES interventions delivered via surface electrodes in adults with kidney failure receiving hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis
exclusion: Studies using single-session NMES, NMES in transient acute dialysis samples, combining NMES with concurrent exercise without a control group, or conducted in non-dialysis chronic kidney disease populations

appraisal.bottom_line: The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effect of NMES on life participation (MD 1.00, 95% CI -3.85 to 5.85) and death (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.01 to 5.26). Low-certainty evidence suggests NMES may result in little to no difference in diastolic blood pressure (MD 2.72, 95% CI -2.85 to 8.29), systolic blood pressure (MD 5.54, 95% CI -4.02 to 15.09), or resting heart rate (MD 4.58, 95% CI -2.67 to 11.82).
appraisal.relevance: While NMES is proposed as an alternative or adjunct to exercise for dialysis patients with muscle wasting, current evidence does not support a clear clinical benefit on critical cardiovascular or patient-centered outcomes.
appraisal.caveat: The certainty of the evidence is low to very low, severely limited by small sample sizes, risk of bias, and imprecision. No studies evaluated peritoneal dialysis patients, and key patient-centered outcomes such as fatigue, pain, and vascular access problems were completely unreported.

articles.authors: Bittencourt JAS, Figueredo AS, Melo NAC, Pereira CL, Moraes YAC et al.
articles.title: Applications of artificial intelligence in chronic kidney disease: a systematic review.
articles.summary: A systematic review of 26 studies published between 2019 and 2025 evaluating the applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in the early diagnosis, prediction, and management of chronic kidney disease (CKD).

pico.population: Patients at risk for or diagnosed with chronic kidney disease
pico.intervention: Artificial intelligence tools (supervised learning and deep learning algorithms)
pico.comparison: Standard clinical care or no AI tool
pico.outcome: Early detection, disease management, and model performance metrics (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity)

inclusion: Studies published between 2019 and 2025 in PubMed and Scopus considering patients at risk for or diagnosed with CKD, AI tools as interventions, and outcomes related to early detection and disease management

appraisal.bottom_line: Supervised and deep learning AI models demonstrate high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity in identifying CKD and its stages. However, methodological weaknesses—particularly the lack of external validation, poor control of confounding factors, and non-standardized datasets—limit their current clinical generalizability.
appraisal.relevance: AI represents a promising strategic tool for early CKD detection and individualized management, but current models are not yet ready for reliable integration into real-world clinical practice.
appraisal.caveat: This is a systematic review of highly heterogeneous, mostly retrospective model-development studies. The lack of external validation and prospective clinical trials means the reported high accuracies may not translate to actual patient care settings.

articles.title: Effectiveness of Nursing and Non-Pharmacological Interventions in Reducing Intradialytic Hypotension Among Haemodialysis Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies evaluating the effectiveness of non-pharmacological and nursing interventions in reducing intradialytic hypotension among adult hemodialysis patients.

pico.intervention: Non-pharmacological interventions (including dialysis technology-based and nurse-led interventions)
pico.outcome: Systolic blood pressure during haemodialysis and incidence of intradialytic hypotension

inclusion: Randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies evaluating non-pharmacological interventions published between January 2000 and July 2025

appraisal.bottom_line: Non-pharmacological interventions, particularly dialysis technology-based approaches, are associated with modest improvements in systolic blood pressure during hemodialysis. However, the overall certainty of the evidence is very low.
appraisal.relevance: Intradialytic hypotension is a common and distressing complication of hemodialysis; non-pharmacological and nurse-led strategies may offer supportive hemodynamic benefits, though clinical efficacy remains unproven.
appraisal.caveat: The primary outcome evaluated was systolic blood pressure, which is a surrogate hemodynamic marker and does not necessarily equate to a reduction in actual clinical events of intradialytic hypotension. The inclusion of quasi-experimental studies and very low certainty of evidence limit the strength of these findings.

articles.authors: Ismail A, Sauriasari R, Yanuar A, Sudiana D, Cokro F
articles.title: Improving Medication Safety in Chronic Kidney Disease Using Rule-Based and Artificial Intelligence-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 RCTs (6 contributing meta-analytic data) evaluating the impact of rule-based and AI/ML-based clinical decision support systems (CDSS) on medication safety in adults with CKD.

pico.population: Adults with CKD or at risk of CKD-related prescribing errors
pico.intervention: Rule-based or AI/ML-based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS)
pico.outcome: Medication safety endpoints (appropriate renal dosing, potentially inappropriate prescribing, medication errors) and EHR documentation of CKD

inclusion: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing rule-based or AI/ML CDSS with usual care among adults with CKD or at risk of CKD-related prescribing errors

appraisal.bottom_line: CDSS improved appropriate renal dosing (RR 1.76; 95% CI 1.13-2.74) and EHR documentation of CKD (RR 1.19; 95% CI 1.07-1.32). However, extreme heterogeneity (I2 = 97%) and a wide 95% prediction interval (0.75-4.14) crossing the null indicate that the dosing benefit is highly context-dependent and not guaranteed in new settings. Clinician compliance was low, ranging from 17% to 74%.
appraisal.relevance: CDSS can assist in reducing prescribing errors and improving CKD documentation, but its real-world effectiveness is hampered by low clinician compliance due to alert fatigue and workflow barriers.
appraisal.caveat: The meta-analysis is limited by extreme statistical heterogeneity (I2 = 97%) and a prediction interval that crosses the null, meaning the intervention's effect is highly variable. Most interventions were interruptive order-entry alerts, which suffer from high override rates.
